# Types

Every Nish type maps 1:1 onto one LLVM first-class type. There is no
boxing, no runtime type tag, no structural subtyping (except
`implements`, below), and no implicit conversion of any kind: two values are
compatible only when their types are identical.

Read from the top down as deep as you need: which type to write, what
behaves differently from TypeScript, how each type sits in memory and
crosses to C, then the exact rules.

## Choosing a type

| To hold | Write |
| --- | --- |
| A whole number | `number`, or `i64` beyond ±2³¹ |
| A fraction | `f64`; `f32` for half the memory or twice the SIMD lanes |
| A byte, or bits that wrap | `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64` |
| True or false | `boolean` |
| Text | `string` |
| A list | `T[]`, or `readonly T[]` when nothing writes it |
| A record | `class C`, or `interface I` |
| One of a fixed set of names | `enum K` |
| A value or nothing | `T \| null` |
| One of several kinds of record | `A \| B`, a [tagged union](#discriminated-unions) |
| A value or an error | `Result<T, E>` |
| A function the caller picks | `(x: T) => U` on a parameter |
| No value | `void`, as a return type |

## Coming from TypeScript

- **`number` is one fixed type.** It is `i32` by default and `f64` under
  `--number-mode f64`; nothing else is ever its lowering. `f64` is available
  in both modes.
- **Nothing converts on its own.** Each numeric type is its own type, so
  `u32 + i32` and `f32 + f64` are type errors. Convert with `toI32`, `toU8`,
  `toF64` and the rest ([Type rules](#type-rules)).
- **Signed overflow panics** ([Semantics decisions](semantics-decisions.md)),
  in `i32` and `i64` alike; `wrappingAdd`, `wrappingSub` and `wrappingMul`
  from [`nish:unsafe`](builtins.md#nishunsafe-unchecked-access-and-defined-wrapping)
  wrap instead. [Unsigned integers](#unsigned-integers) always wrap. An
  `i64` takes a literal only by context.
- **Strings are immutable.** Sharing one is always safe, and nothing is ever
  copied.
- **An array has one element type**, and every index is bounds-checked.
  `readonly T[]` refuses every write ([Readonly arrays](builtins.md#readonly-arrays)).
  `Int32Array`, `Float32Array`, `Float64Array` and `BigInt64Array` are only
  other names for `i32[]`, `f32[]`, `f64[]` and `i64[]` (`sameType` holds,
  and `new Int32Array(n)` is `new Array<i32>(n)`), except that a receiver
  spelled with one has no `push` or `pop`, as in TypeScript
  ([Typed-array names have no `push` or `pop`](builtins.md#typed-array-names-have-no-push-or-pop)).
- **Only a class, interface, array, string or function reference can be
  `null`.** A nullable value allows only `=== null` / `!== null`, assignment,
  narrowing and a `??` default ([Nullable types](#nullable-types)); a nullable
  function reference is the tag `0` ([Function references](declarations.md#function-references)).
- **An `enum` is its own type**, not a spelling of `i32`: `sameType` fails
  against every other type ([Enums](declarations.md#enums)).
- **A record's type has a name.** Its fields are declared once, in an
  `interface` or a `class`; an inline object type, `{ x: i32 }`, is refused
  wherever a type is written, and `type` only renames a type that already
  exists ([Interfaces and object literals](declarations.md#interfaces-and-object-literals),
  [Type aliases](declarations.md#type-aliases)).
- **A function reports failure with a `Result`**, the only way it can; the
  payload is unreachable until the discriminant is tested
  ([Result and error handling](result-and-error-handling.md)).
- **A function type** written inline on a parameter of a top-level
  function names the callee chosen at each call
  ([Function parameters](declarations.md#function-parameters)); anywhere else it is the type
  of a reference to a capture-free top-level function, which can be held,
  passed, called and compared, nothing else
  ([Function references](declarations.md#function-references)).

## In memory and in C

A number, a `boolean` or an `enum` is a plain value. The C column is the
type `--emit-header` writes; a dash means the type cannot cross to C.

| Type | LLVM | Size / align | C |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `i32`, `number` | `i32` | 4 / 4 | `int32_t` |
| `f64`, `number` in f64 mode | `double` | 8 / 8 | `double` |
| `f32` | `float` | 4 / 4 | `float` |
| `i64` | `i64` | 8 / 8 | `int64_t` |
| `u8` | `i8` | 1 / 1 | `uint8_t` |
| `u16` | `i16` | 2 / 2 | `uint16_t` |
| `u32` | `i32` | 4 / 4 | `uint32_t` |
| `u64` | `i64` | 8 / 8 | `uint64_t` |
| `boolean` | `i1` | 1 / 1 | `bool` |
| `enum K` | `i32` | 4 / 4 | — |
| `void` | `void` | — | `void` |

- Signed integers are two's-complement, and floats IEEE-754. An unsigned
  type shares the LLVM type of its signed twin, and its signedness lives in
  the operations ([Unsigned integers](#unsigned-integers)). `i64` and `u64`
  cross to JavaScript as a `bigint`.
- A `boolean` is `zeroext` at the ABI boundary.
- `K.A` is the member's integer, so nothing is emitted for an `enum`
  declaration.

Every other type is a pointer, 8 bytes and 8-aligned, to:

- **`string`**, LLVM `i8*`: `{ i64 len, i8 data[len], i8 0 }`, 8-aligned and
  NUL-terminated, so `data` is a C string, and `len` is the UTF-8 byte
  length. Literals are module constants; every other string lives in the
  arena. In C, a `const nish_str *` parameter and a `nish_str *` result.
- **`T[]`**, LLVM `%struct.nish_array*`: a 24-byte header,
  `{ i64 len, i64 cap, i8* data }`, where `data` holds `cap` elements of
  `sizeof(T)`. In C, a `const nish_array *` parameter the function only
  reads, and a `nish_array *` parameter it writes through or a `nish_array *`
  result.
- **`readonly T[]`**: the same array, a `const nish_array *` parameter in C.
- **`Int32Array`, `Float32Array`, `Float64Array`, `BigInt64Array`**: the
  arrays they name. They name the JS typed array a host passes
  ([wp8-interop.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp8-interop.md)). An unsigned array crosses to a host as
  `Uint8Array`, `Uint16Array`, `Uint32Array` or `BigUint64Array`
  ([wp30-bytes-interop.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp30-bytes-interop.md)), but those four are
  **not** spellings in the language: a program writes `u8[]`.
- **`class C`, `interface I`**, LLVM `%struct.C*`:
  `%struct.C = type { fields in declaration order }`, laid out as clang lays
  out the same C struct, with no header and no vtable. An object is arena- or
  stack-allocated ([Memory model](semantics-decisions.md#memory-model)). Not in C.
- **`T | null`**: whatever `T` points to; `null` is the constant `null`. Not
  in C.
- **`A | B`**, LLVM `%union.tagged*`: `%union.tagged = type { i32 }`, the tag
  every variant begins with. A variant converts by a `bitcast`, and only the
  tag is read ([Discriminated unions](#discriminated-unions)). Not in C.
- **`Result<T, E>`**, LLVM `%struct.nish_result.<T>.<E>*`:
  `{ i1 ok, T value, E error }`, one struct per pair of payload types, laid
  out as clang lays out the same C struct. It is **passed and returned** as
  one `i64` when both payloads are scalars of at most 4 bytes, and as
  `{ i1, i32, i32 }`, the tag and one slot per arm, between two non-exported
  functions of one module. In C, a `nish_result_<T>_<E>_word` by value, and a
  `struct nish_result_<T>_<E> *` otherwise.

A function type, `(x: T) => U`, written inline on a parameter of a
top-level function is no value at all: it has no LLVM type and no parameter,
and the callee is compiled into the instantiation's body as a direct call.
Anywhere else it is a function reference, LLVM `i32`, 4 / 4: a tag naming
one of the program's functions of that signature, never an address
([Function references](declarations.md#function-references)). Not in C.

Sources: `src/types.ts` (`TypeTable.llvmType`, `alignOf`; a type is
interned, and two types are the same type exactly when they are the same
`i32`),
`src/interop-abi.ts` (`cType`); `tests/cases/i64_basic`, `f64_mode`,
`str_literal`, `arr_literal`, `cls_point`; the ten-struct layout test
`tests/layout/structs.ts` (offsets and `sizeof` cross-checked against clang,
[wp2-classes.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp2-classes.md#layout)).

## Type rules

- **Accepted type syntax**: `number`, `i32`, `i64`, `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`,
  `f32`, `f64`, `boolean`,
  `string`, `void`, `T[]`, `Array<T>` (exactly one type argument:
  `` `Array` needs exactly one type argument ``), `readonly T[]` and
  `ReadonlyArray<T>` ([Readonly arrays](builtins.md#readonly-arrays)), `Int32Array`,
  `Float32Array`, `Float64Array`, `BigInt64Array` (no type argument:
  `` `Float64Array` takes no type argument (it is an alias of `f64[]`) ``,
  `tests/cases/reject_arr_typed_view_type_annotation_arg`; a `Float64Array`
  is an `f64[]` wherever one is expected and vice versa,
  `tests/cases/arr_typed_views`, `reject_arr_typed_view_mismatch`), the name of
  a `type` alias or a numeric `enum` declared or imported in the module
  ([Type aliases](declarations.md#type-aliases), [Enums](declarations.md#enums)), one of that enum's
  members as a type, `Kind.If` ([Enums](declarations.md#enums)), and the
  name of a class or interface declared or imported in the module. Anything else is
  `` Unsupported type `...` `` / `` Unsupported type reference `...` ``
  (`src/annotations.ts`; `tests/cases/reject_union_type`, `reject_function_type`).
  `keyof T` is one of those, `` Unsupported type `keyof T` (Phase 1 supports
  number, i32, i64, u8, u16, u32, u64, f32, f64, boolean, string, void) ``
  (NL2038), and it is refused in a generic declaration nothing instantiates too, because the
  rule is a pass over the whole module rather than a step in resolving an
  annotation (`reject_type_keyof`, `reject_type_keyof_template`). `keyof` is
  the operator only before a type on its own line, so a class a program names
  `keyof` is still a type everywhere else (`tests/parser/names-declarations.ts`).
  `T | null` (or `null | T`) is accepted when `T` is a class, interface,
  array, string or [function reference](declarations.md#function-references) type; a scalar is
  `` `i32 | null` is not supported: only class, interface, array, and string types can be nullable (a scalar has no null value) ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_nullable_scalar`). A type may be **parenthesised**, and
  `(T | null)[]` is where it matters: `T | null[]` groups the other way and
  means "a `T`, or an array of `null`". The parentheses only group — the type
  inside them is the type — so `(A | B)[]` is held to the union rules as
  `A | B` is (`tests/cases/cls_parenthesized_type`, `reject_paren_union_type`).
  A union of tagged classes and interfaces is a
  [discriminated union](#discriminated-unions).
- **No implicit conversion.** `const y: f64 = x` with `x: number` in i32
  mode is `Cannot initialize f64 variable ... with i32` *(CLI only)*;
  `x + n` with `x: i64`, `n: number` is rejected
  (`tests/cases/reject_i64_mixed`); convert explicitly with `toI32`,
  `toI64`, `toU8`, `toU16`, `toU32`, `toU64`, `toF32`, `toF64`
  (`tests/cases/conversions`, `u_conv_roundtrip`, `f32_conversions`). Width and
  signedness are part of the
  type, so `f32 + f64` is
  `` Operator `+` requires two operands of the same numeric type ... got f32 and f64 ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_f32_mixed`) and, even when the LLVM type is shared, `u32 + i32` is
  `` Operator `+` requires two operands of the same numeric type ... got u32 and i32 ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_u_mixed_signedness`), and so is `u8 * u32`
  (`tests/cases/reject_u_mixed_widths`).
- **Field and element types** may be any type except `void`
  (`Array elements cannot be void`, `... cannot have type void`).
  Arrays of arrays (`tests/cases/arr_nested`), arrays of strings
  (`tests/cases/arr_strings`), arrays of class instances and class fields
  of array type work *(CLI only)*.
- **`integer<Lo, Hi>` is a ranged integer** ([wp31-ranged-integers.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp31-ranged-integers.md)):
  an `i32` the compiler knows lies in `[Lo, Hi]`. It is an `i32` in the IR, in
  memory and at the ABI, in both number modes, and `tsc` reads it as a
  `number` alias (`runtime/nish.d.ts`). `integer<0, 0xFF>` and
  `integer<0, 255>` are one type, spelled `integer<0, 255>` in a diagnostic and
  mangled `rng.p0.p255` in a symbol (`rng.m128.p127` for `integer<-128, 127>`),
  so `Box<integer<0, 255>>` is `%struct.Box$rng.p0.p255`
  (`tests/cases/rng_param`, `rng_generic`).
  - **The bounds** are two integer literals, a sign allowed, with
    `Lo <= Hi` and both in `i32`. Each other spelling is refused:
    `` `integer` needs exactly two bounds, e.g. `integer<0, 255>` ``
    (`reject_rng_arity`, `reject_integer_use`);
    ``A bound of `integer<Lo, Hi>` must be an integer literal, got `MAX` ``,
    a constant or a type (`reject_rng_bound_not_literal`,
    `reject_rng_bound_type`);
    ``Non-integer literal `1.5` where a bound of `integer<Lo, Hi>` is expected``
    (`reject_rng_bound_float`);
    `` `integer<10, 0>` is an empty range `` (`reject_rng_empty`); and
    ``Bound `4294967295` of `integer<Lo, Hi>` is outside i32``
    (`reject_rng_bound_i32`, `reject_rng_bound_i32_negative`). A numeric
    literal type is parsed wherever a type is and is legal only as one of
    these bounds: `const x: 5` and `Box<3>` are
    ``A literal type `5` is only allowed as a bound of `integer<Lo, Hi>` ``
    (`reject_rng_literal_type`, `reject_rng_literal_type_argument`).
  - **Entering a range is checked.** An annotated initialiser, an assignment
    (`=`, the compound forms, `++` and `--`), an argument to a function, a
    method or a constructor, a `return`, a field or object-literal field, an
    array-literal element, an element store and `push` are *entries*. The
    source must be an `i32` or another ranged type — a `u8` is not an
    `integer<0, 255>` (`reject_rng_from_u8`), and under `--number-mode f64` a
    `number` is an `f64` that enters through `toI32(x)` (`reject_rng_from_f64`).
    A literal inside the range and a value of a range inside this one cost
    nothing; a literal outside it is
    ``Literal `12` is outside the range of integer<0, 9>``
    (`reject_rng_literal_outside`, `reject_rng_literal_outside_negative`).
    Anything else is compared once and the program panics outside the range,
    printing `value out of range: expected integer<0, 255>` and exiting 1
    (`rng_param`, `rng_entries`, `rng_bitwise`, `rng_entry_panic`,
    `rng_entry_range_panic`, `rng_entry_push_panic`, `rng_entry_bitwise_panic`). The check is the type's
    meaning, so `uncheckedGet` and `uncheckedSet` keep it, and a `wrapping*`
    call changes only the arithmetic before it. Under Node nothing is checked, which
    [RUN_UNDER_NODE.md](../../RUN_UNDER_NODE.md#what-stays-divergent) records.
  - **An entry the compiler can prove is free** (WP31 §8). The bounds proof of
    [Element access](expressions.md#element-access) judges each entry where the value is
    computed, and writes no compare where it already places the value inside
    the range. Two sources can be proven. A local is proven one end at a
    time: the lower end when `Lo` is `-2147483648`, or `Lo <= 0` and the local
    is known non-negative; the upper end when `Hi` is `2147483647`, or the
    local is known below `Hi + 1` — by a loop condition, a guard that reaches
    the entry, a literal it was bound to, or its own declared range. And
    `toI32(x)` of a `u8`, a `u16` or a ranged value lands in `x`'s declared
    range, so `const r: integer<0, 255> = toI32(b)` costs nothing for a `u8`
    `b`. `for (let i = 0; i < 256; i++) { const b: integer<0, 255> = i }` is
    the shape §7 recommends, and the loop condition proves it
    (`tests/cases/perf_rng_quiet`); so is a call that hands a loop counter to a
    ranged parameter, which leaves wp31 §12's `getByte` program with no check
    at all (`perf_rng_getbyte`). A lower end above zero is never proven
    from a guard, because the proof records no lower bound but zero, and the
    sum a compound assignment or an increment stores back is never proven at
    all; both keep their check. A check that survives inside a loop is a
    performance warning ([Diagnostics](semantics-decisions.md#diagnostics-and-debugging-flags)), and a counter declared
    with a range is the loop that warns and then panics
    (`perf_rng_counter`).
  - **Leaving a range is free.** Every operator reads a ranged value as `i32`,
    so `r + 1` is an `i32`, `r < 9` compares two `i32`s and `toI64(r)` is a
    `sext`; mixing one with an `i32` is never an error, and nothing computes a
    range. The range survives where nothing is computed: a `const` without an
    annotation keeps it and a `let` widens to `i32` (`rng_widen`); a read of a
    ranged field, element or result keeps it; and a type argument keeps it, so
    `identity(r)` is `identity<integer<0, 9>>` (`rng_generic`). A counter
    declared with a range fails its last `i++`, which is why the range goes on
    the value used rather than on the counter (`rng_entry_panic`).
  - **Where a range may not go.** A `declare function` may not mention one,
    because the C side never promised it (`reject_rng_declare_function`,
    `reject_rng_declare_function_return`), and `new Array<integer<1, 9>>(n)` is
    refused because its zero fill is outside the range
    (`reject_rng_array_zero_fill`). Under `-g` a ranged type is a
    `DW_TAG_typedef` of `int` named `integer<0, 255>` (`dbg_rng`).
  - **The name.** `integer` is on the list of built-in type names, so
    `type integer = …` and `enum integer` are refused the way `type string = …`
    is (`reject_integer_alias`, `reject_integer_enum`). A class, interface or
    function may not take it either, because `integer<0, 255>` would then mean
    two things in the module that declared one:
    `` `integer` is reserved for ranged integers (`integer<Lo, Hi>`) and cannot be declared as a class ``
    (`reject_integer_class`, `reject_integer_interface`,
    `reject_integer_function`). A module constant or a local called `integer`
    is a value, not a type, and is still accepted.

## Numeric literals

**A separator goes between two digits and nowhere else**, as in TypeScript.
`1_000_000`, `0xFF_FF` and `1_234.5_6` are the values their digits spell, and
so is `1e1_0` in an exponent (`tests/cases/math_numeric_separators`). Any
other `_` is refused by the lexer with TypeScript's words, one error for the
whole literal: after a radix prefix (`0x_FF`,
`tests/cases/reject_separator_after_prefix`), at the end (`10_`,
`reject_separator_trailing`), either side of the point (`1_.5`, `1._5`:
`reject_separator_before_dot`, `reject_separator_after_dot`), straight after
the exponent marker or its sign (`1e_5`, `1e+_5`, `reject_separator_exponent`),
before the BigInt suffix (`0xFF_n`, `reject_separator_before_bigint_suffix`)
and after a leading zero (`0_1`, `reject_separator_leading_zero`) are all
`` Numeric separators are not allowed here `` (TS6188), and two in a row
(`1__0`, `0xF__F`, `reject_separator_doubled`) is
`` Multiple consecutive numeric separators are not permitted `` (TS6189). The
parser still reads the literal, so the next token does not cost a second
error, and a bound of a ranged type is refused the same way
(`integer<0, 0x_FF>`, `reject_separator_ranged_bound`).

**A decimal literal does not start with `0` and another digit**, as in
TypeScript, and as in a JavaScript module, where Node refuses one as a
`SyntaxError`. `0`, `0.5` and `0e1` are legal, and so is every radix prefix
(`tests/cases/leading_zero_legal`). A run of octal digits after the zero is a
legacy octal literal: `017`, and `017.5` or `07_1` with it, are
`` Octal literals are not allowed. Use the syntax '0o17' `` (TS1121), naming the
`0o` spelling of those digits (`tests/cases/reject_leading_zero_octal`). Any
other, such as `09`, `08.5` or `09e1`, is
`` Decimals with leading zeros are not allowed `` (TS1489,
`reject_leading_zero_decimal`). The lexer refuses it and it costs one error,
as a misplaced separator does. Before issue #271, `017` compiled as seventeen.
There are two differences from `tsc`. `tsc` reads `017.5` as two tokens and
reports a second error for the `.5`, but the lexer reports one error for the
whole literal. And `-017` suggests `0o17`, not `-0o17`, because the lexer does
not see the sign.

**Every spelling is read at the value it spells, in every numeric type**,
as TypeScript reads it (#267): `0b1010` is 10, `0o17` is 15, `1_000` is 1000
and `1e5` is 100000 as an `i32`, an `i64`, an `f64`, a module constant or a
bound of `integer<Lo, Hi>` (`tests/cases/literal_spellings`). A binary or
octal literal past 2^53 rounds once, to the double TypeScript reads. An
exponent is an integer when its value is one, so `100e-2` is the integer 1 and
`1e-1` in an integer position is `` Non-integer literal `1e-1` where i32 is
expected `` (`reject_literal_exponent_fraction`); a point always spells a
float. The range rules below read the same value, so `1e10` and a 33-bit
`0b` literal are `` Literal `1e10` does not fit in i32 ``
(`reject_literal_exponent_overflow`, `reject_literal_binary_overflow`), and an
`i64` module constant past 2^53 is refused as an `i64` literal is
(`reject_literal_const_precision`).

A numeric literal has the mode's default type (`i32`, or `f64` in f64 mode)
unless its *immediate* context demands another numeric type, in which case it
takes that type (`src/expressions.ts`, `checkNumericLiteral`;
`tests/cases/i64_basic`, `math_i32`, `conversions`):

| Context | Example | Literal type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| annotated initializer | `let x: i64 = 5` | `i64` |
| `return` | `return 5` in a function returning `i64` | `i64` |
| argument to a user function | `square(5)` with `x: i64` | `i64` |
| other operand of a binary operator with a known type | `x * 2`, `2 * x`, `x < 5`, `x = 5` | the other operand's type |
| `Math.min` / `Math.max` | `Math.max(x, 0)` | the other operand's type |
| f64-only `Math.*`, `toF64` | `Math.sqrt(2)`, `toF64(3)` | `f64` |
| `toF32` | `toF32(2.75)` | `f32` |
| `process.exit` | `process.exit(1)` in f64 mode | `i32` |
| `Number` | `Number(2.5)` in i32 mode | `f64` |
| element of an array literal whose own context is a `T[]` | `const bytes: u8[] = [0, 255]` | `u8` |
| a class field's literal initializer | `b: u8 = 255` | `u8` |
| argument to a constructor | `new Pixel(255, 0, 0)` | the parameter's type |
| a field or element assignment target | `p.b = 255`, `bytes[i] = 255` | the field's / element's type |
| a ternary arm, from the conditional's own context | `const x: f64 = c ? 1.5 : 2.5` | `f64` (`tests/cases/f64_ternary_literal`) |

`-5` and `(5)` count as the literal, on **either** side of a binary operator:
`-1 / z` and `(1) / z` with `z: f64` type their literal from `z` exactly as
`1 / z` does, and so do `-1 * big` on an `i64` and `-1 < z`
(`tests/cases/math_literal_operand_forms`). The other operand still has to be
one of the shapes "known type" names below, so `-1 * (cp >> 6)` in f64 mode is
refused for the same reason `0xc0 | (cp >> 6)` is
(`tests/cases/reject_neg_literal_unpeekable`). **The table is the whole list**, so a
position that is not on it leaves the literal at the mode's default however
obvious the intended type looks: an object literal's property value is not on
it, so `const p: Pixel = { b: 255 }` is `` Field `b` of `Pixel` expects a value
of type u8, got i32 `` and has to be written `toU8(255)`
(`tests/cases/reject_struct_field_u8`, and `reject_struct_field_f64` for the
same position in f64 mode); nor is a `Result` payload, so `Ok(3)` for a
`Result<i32, string>` is refused in f64 mode
(`tests/cases/reject_res_ok_f64`), as `unwrapOr`'s fallback is
(`reject_res_unwrap_or_f64`); and nor is a **method's** argument, which is why
the table says a user *function* and a constructor — `b.get(-1)` on a method
whose parameter is an `i32` is an f64 in f64 mode
(`tests/cases/reject_method_arg_literal`).
`xs.push(3)` and `xs.indexOf(3)` are on the list only through a receiver that
is a plain name: `b.xs.push(0)` is not (`reject_push_field_literal`). "Known type" means an already-checked
left operand, a variable, a field or element of one of those, or a call to a
user function or to
`toI32/toI64/toU8/toU16/toU32/toU64/toF64`. Only the literal's *immediate* context counts: in i32
mode `const f: f64 = 0.1 + 0.2` is rejected because `0.1` is an operand of
`+` whose other operand has no known type yet; write `const a: f64 = 0.1;
const f = a + 0.2` *(CLI only)*. The same rule refuses `const b: u8 = 1 + 2`,
which is a sum of two `i32` literals rather than a literal in a `u8` context
(`tests/cases/reject_bin_operand_context`), and `0xc0 | (cp >> 6)` in f64 mode,
because a shift is not one of the shapes "known type" names however plainly it
is an integer: give it a name first, or write `toI32(0xc0)`. A literal in an integer context must be integral
(`` Non-integer literal `1.5` where i64 is expected ``,
`tests/cases/reject_i64_literal_float`); in an `i64` context it must also be
at most 2^53 in magnitude (`` exceeds 2^53 and cannot be written exactly ``,
`tests/cases/reject_i64_literal_precision`; an unsigned context has the same
rule, `reject_u64_literal_precision`) because a numeric literal is read as a
double, as TypeScript reads it, so a larger one is already rounded. Every one of these messages quotes the
literal **as it is written**, not as the parser cooked it: `0x1FF` reads back
as `0x1FF` and a rounded literal as the digits in the file. The one exception
is a separator, which the parser drops, so `1_000_000_000_000` in an `i32`
context reads back as `` Literal `1000000000000` does not fit in i32 ``. In an *unsigned* context it must also be non-negative
and fit the width: `const b: u8 = -1` is
`` Negative literal `-1` where u8 is expected (u8 is unsigned) ``
(`tests/cases/reject_u_negative_literal`) and `const b: u8 = 256` is
`` Literal `256` does not fit in u8 ``
(`tests/cases/reject_u_literal_too_wide`). The largest `u64` values are past
2^53 and cannot be written at all; build them arithmetically
(`toU64(0) - toU64(1)` is 2^64 - 1, `tests/cases/u_print`). The same holds for
the `i64` minimum, -2^63: `-9223372036854775808` is refused like any literal
past 2^53 (NL2055), although 2^63 happens to be an exact double and its
negation fits. The 2^53 bound is what keeps every literal exact in both
readings, and admitting this value would be a one-literal exception to it for
no gain: in the TypeScript reading `i64` is `number`, so the value is a double
there anyway (NL8009). Build it from the widest literal instead:
`const lo: i64 = -9007199254740992; const min: i64 = lo << 10;` is -2^63
(`tests/cases/neg_literal_i64_min`).

## Unsigned integers

`u8`, `u16`, `u32` and `u64` are unsigned integers with wrapping arithmetic.
LLVM has no unsigned types, so they lower to `i8`, `i16`, `i32` and `i64` and
the signedness lives entirely in the *operations*; representing an unsigned
value therefore costs nothing at all, and a `u8` field packs a struct as
tightly as a C `uint8_t` does.

| Operation | On `i32` / `i64` | On `u8` / `u16` / `u32` / `u64` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `+ - *`, unary `-`, `++`/`--` | `add nsw` `sub nsw` `mul nsw` where proven to fit, else `llvm.s{add,sub,mul}.with.overflow` and a branch to the panic; plain through `wrappingAdd`/`wrappingSub`/`wrappingMul` from `nish:unsafe` | the same instructions, never flagged or checked: unsigned overflow wraps in both modes |
| `/ %` | `sdiv` / `srem` after a two-part divisor check | `udiv` / `urem` after a single compare ([Checked integer division](expressions.md#checked-integer-division)) |
| `< <= > >=` | `icmp slt sle sgt sge` | `icmp ult ule ugt uge` |
| `>>` | `ashr` | `lshr` |
| `>>>` | `lshr` | `lshr` — the same instruction, so the two are synonyms |
| `=== !==` | `icmp eq` / `icmp ne` | identical (the bits decide) |
| widening conversion | `sext` | `zext` |
| narrowing conversion | `trunc` | `trunc` |
| to / from `f64` | `sitofp` / `llvm.fptosi.sat` | `uitofp` / `llvm.fptoui.sat` |
| `Math.abs` | `llvm.abs` | nothing: the value is already its own magnitude |
| `Math.min` / `Math.max` | `llvm.smin` / `llvm.smax` | `llvm.umin` / `llvm.umax` |
| `console.log(x)`, `` `${x}` `` | `nish_str_from_i32` / `_i64` | `zext` to i64, then `nish_str_from_u64` |
| overflow | a panic, "attempt to add with overflow", exit 1, except a `nish:unsafe` `wrapping*` call | nothing, in either mode: unsigned overflow is defined as wrapping |

The consequences worth knowing:

- **A value above `INT_MAX` behaves.** `const big: u32 = 4000000000` compares,
  divides and prints as four billion, where the same bits in an `i32` are
  -294967296 (`tests/cases/u_compare_above_intmax`, `u_udiv_urem`, `u_print`;
  `tests/differential/corpus/u_div_cmp`).
- **Division is cheaper.** Unsigned division has no overflow case, so its
  check is one compare instead of three plus an `and` and an `or`
  (`tests/cases/u_div_one_check`).
- **Overflow wraps**, and unlike the signed types it wraps in *every* mode:
  `(255: u8) + 1` is `0` and `(0: u8) - 1` is `255` (`tests/cases/u_arith_wrap`,
  `tests/differential/corpus/u_wrap`). No `nuw` is ever emitted, neither is
  `nsw`, and nothing is checked: wrapping is what hashing and bit-packing are
  written against, and it is half the reason the unsigned widths exist.
- **Mixing is an error.** `u32` and `i32` are different types even though both
  are `i32` in the IR, and so are `u8` and `u32`; there is no implicit
  conversion anywhere in this language
  (`tests/cases/reject_u_mixed_signedness`, `reject_u_mixed_widths`).
- **`i32 >>> n` still yields the raw bits read as signed** — `-1 >>> 0` is
  `-1` here where JavaScript gives `4294967295` — because an `i32` is the only
  place the result could go. That is now something to avoid rather than
  something to live with: use `u32` and the answer is `4294967295`
  (`tests/cases/u_shift_logical`, `u_conv_roundtrip`;
  `tests/differential/corpus/u_convert_shift`).

## `f32`

`f32` is 32-bit IEEE-754, LLVM's `float`. Every operation is the instruction
`f64` already uses, one width down — `fadd`/`fsub`/`fmul`/`fdiv`/`frem`,
`fcmp o*`, `fneg` — and float division is never checked, exactly as for `f64`
(`tests/cases/f32_arith`). It exists because a struct of `f32` is half the
footprint of one of `f64` and gives twice the SIMD lane count:
`class Vec3 { x: f32; y: f32; z: f32; hits: u32 }` is 16 bytes where three
doubles alone would be 24 (`tests/cases/f32_struct`).

- **It is not `number`.** `number` is `i32` or `f64` depending on
  `--number-mode`; `f32` is always spelled `f32`, and there is no implicit
  widening: `f32 + f64` is
  `` Operator `+` requires two operands of the same numeric type ... got f32 and f64 ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_f32_mixed`). Convert with `toF32` / `toF64`.
- **A literal takes `f32` from context** the same way it takes `f64`
  (`const tenth: f32 = 0.1`), and is rounded to the nearest float when it is
  emitted. LLVM writes a `float` constant with the 64-bit hex of the double it
  equals and requires that double to be exactly a float, so `0.1` as an `f32`
  is `float 0x3FB99999A0000000` — the double nearest to `(float) 0.1` — and
  not the `f64` spelling `0x3FB999999999999A` (`tests/cases/f32_constant`).
- **Printing gives JavaScript's digits for the float's value.**
  `console.log(x)` and `` `${x}` `` widen with `fpext` and reuse
  `nish_str_from_f64`, so `const tenth: f32 = 0.1` prints
  `0.10000000149011612` where the same literal as an `f64` prints `0.1`
  (`tests/cases/f32_print`; `tests/differential/corpus/f32_round`).
- **The f64-only `Math` functions stay f64-only.** `Math.sqrt(x)` on an `f32`
  is `` `Math.sqrt` requires an f64 argument, got f32 ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_f32_math_sqrt`); `Math.abs`, `Math.min` and `Math.max`
  do work, through `llvm.fabs.f32` and the float compare-and-select `min` and
  `max` lower to, and so does `Math.sign`.
- **`Float32Array` is `f32[]`**, one more typed-array alias with no second
  layout, so a Node host's `Float32Array` crosses the boundary the way an
  `Int32Array` already does.

## Shifts

`<<`, `>>` and `>>>` take two operands of one *integer* type and produce that
type. There is no implicit conversion, so the shift amount has the same type as
the value (`` Operator `>>` requires two operands of the same integer type, got
u32 and i32 ``, `tests/cases/reject_u_shift_mixed`), and `f64` has no shift at
all.

`>>` is an arithmetic shift on a signed type (`ashr`, sign bit replicated) and
a logical one on an unsigned type (`lshr`, zeros in); `>>>` is always `lshr`,
so on an unsigned type the two operators are synonyms and code that is generic
over a width may spell either (`tests/cases/u_shift_logical`).

The count is **masked to the operand width** rather than left undefined, which
is what makes `x << 33` mean `x << 1` instead of the poison LLVM produces for a
shift at or beyond the width. The mask is `31` at 32 bits and `63` at 64,
matching JavaScript; `u8` and `u16` mask to `7` and `15`, their own widths,
since JavaScript has no narrow unsigned type to be compatible with
(`tests/cases/bit_shift_narrow`). A literal count is masked in the emitter and
written out already masked, so `x << 3` is one instruction and no `and` reaches
the IR; only a computed count costs the mask
([Semantics decisions](semantics-decisions.md)).

## Nullable types

`T | null` is available for `T` a class, interface, array, string, or
function reference (`tests/cases/mem_nullable`;
[wp6-memory.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp6-memory.md#4-t--null)). For a pointer type it is the same
LLVM pointer type as `T` with the constant `null` as one more
value, so nothing is boxed; `null` takes its type from context. A
[function reference](declarations.md#function-references) may be nullable too: it is an
`i32` tag, and `null` is tag 0, which names no function
(`tests/cases/fnref_nullable`).

- **Where `null` may appear**: an annotated initializer
  (`let p: Node | null = null`), a field initializer (`next: Node | null = null`),
  `return` in a function returning `T | null`, an argument, a field or
  element store, an object literal property, `push`, and a ternary arm
  (`c ? p : null` is `T | null`). A `T` is accepted wherever `T | null` is
  expected; the reverse is `` `null` is not a Node; declare the type as `Node | null` ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_null_to_nonnull`).
- **`new Array<T | null>(n)`** is allowed: the zero fill *is* `null`
  (`tests/cases/mem_nullable`).
- **Comparison**: `p === null`, `p !== null`, `null === p` are pointer
  compares (`icmp eq ... null`). Two nullable values cannot be compared with
  each other (`` Cannot compare two `string | null` values; compare each with `null` ``,
  `tests/cases/reject_null_compare_two`), and neither can a nullable and a
  plain `T` *(CLI only)*: narrow first.
- **Narrowing** (`src/expressions.ts`): inside the region a condition
  guards, a nullable *variable* (a local or parameter, never a property
  path) reads as `T`:

  | Form | Where `p` is `T` |
  | --- | --- |
  | `if (p !== null) A else B` | in `A`; and after the `if` when `B` cannot fall through |
  | `if (p === null) A else B` | in `B`; and after the `if` when `A` cannot fall through (`return`, `break`, `continue`, `process.exit`, `panic`) |
  | `while (p !== null) A`, `for (...; p !== null; ...) A` | in `A`, on every iteration |
  | `p !== null && e`, `p === null \|\| e` | in `e` |
  | `p !== null ? a : b` | in `a` (and in `b` for `=== null`) |
  | `!cond`, `(cond)`, `a && b`, `a \|\| b` | composed as expected |

  A narrowing ends at any assignment to the variable (`cur = cur.next` reads
  the narrowed `cur` on the right and then drops it) and before a loop whose
  body, condition, or update assigns the variable, because the second
  iteration sees the assigned value (`tests/cases/reject_null_narrowing_assigned`;
  `reject_null_narrowing_leaks` for a use after the guarded block). Inside an
  `&&` or `||` chain the same holds operand by operand: an operand that
  assigns the variable ends its narrowing for every operand after it and for
  the region the chain guards, so `p !== null && g((p = null) === null) && p.v`
  is refused, and a test after the assignment narrows again
  (`tests/cases/reject_null_narrowing_assigned_in_chain`, `res_proof_consumers`).
  Constants and parameters keep their narrowing for the whole region.
  Property paths are not narrowed: `if (n.next !== null) n.next.v` is
  rejected; copy into a local first *(CLI only)*.
- **`undefined`** is not a value of `T | null`, but the same narrowing rules
  hold for a `const` bound to `Map.get`, with `undefined` in place of `null`
  (WP32, [`Map` and `Set`](builtins.md#map-and-set)).
- **Access** to a field, method, element, or `.length` on an un-narrowed
  nullable is `` Cannot read property `value` of `Node | null`; check for null first ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_null_field_access`).
- **A default**: `a ?? d` on a `T | null` answers `a` where it is not `null`
  and `d` where it is, and runs `d` only then, as TypeScript does: `null` is
  nullish, so no `undefined` is involved. Its type is `T` when `d` is a `T`,
  as `tsc` types it, so the result needs no narrowing; a `d` that may itself
  be `null` keeps the `T | null` (`nullish_nullable`,
  `nullish_nullable_default_null`). `d` takes its context from `T`, so
  `xs ?? []` and an object literal need no annotation; a bare `null`, or a
  ternary that may answer one, is checked into `T | null`
  (`nullish_nullable_default_context`). The left operand is read once, so a
  property path works here although it never narrows: `cur = cur.next ?? cur`
  (`nullish_nullable_field`). A default that cannot have an effect, a literal
  or a name, is one `select`; any other is a branch to `nullish.default` and
  a `phi`. A `new` in the default goes wherever the `??` goes, as a ternary's
  arm does (`nullish_nullable_escapes`), and an arena block is held to both
  operands (`reject_using_arena_nullish`). `d` must be a `T` or a `T | null`:
  `` The right operand of `??` stands in for a missing value, so it must be `string`, the type of the value on its left; got `i32` ``
  (`reject_nullish_nullable_default_type`). The left operand may not be an
  element read, because past the end of the array Node reads `undefined` and
  answers `d` while the bounds check panics:
  `` `??` cannot default an element read: past the end of the array, JavaScript answers the default and Nish panics (test the index against `length`, or read the element into a `const` first) ``
  (`reject_nullish_element`). A left operand that cannot be `null` (a scalar,
  or a nullable already narrowed to `T`) keeps Phase 0's refusal,
  `` Nullish coalescing `??` is forbidden in Nish (narrow with `!== null` instead) ``
  (`reject_nullish`, `reject_nullish_nullable`).
- **An optional chain**: `a?.b?.c ?? d` reads each link only where the
  receiver before its `?.` is not `null`, and answers `d` where one is, as
  TypeScript does. A `?.` is allowed only in a chain whose value is the left
  operand of a `??`, so `undefined`, which `a?.b` answers on its own, is never
  a value: anywhere else, a `const`, an argument, a template hole, an
  assignment target or behind a parenthesis that ends the chain, it is
  `` `?.` is allowed only in a chain that ends in `??`, whose default stands in when a link is `null`: write `a?.b ?? d`, or narrow with `!== null` ``
  (`reject_optional_chain`, `reject_optional_chain_paren`,
  `reject_optional_chain_argument`, `reject_optional_chain_assign`,
  `reject_optional_chain_template`). A link reads a field, a string's or an
  array's `length`, or calls a method, and its receiver is read as `T`
  (`optional_chain_field`, `optional_chain_order`,
  `optional_chain_generic`, `tests/link/optional_chain_modules`). The chain's value is its last link's, typed with
  the default as a `T | null` is above, so a number at the end works:
  `o?.next?.id ?? -1` is an `i32`. Only a `?.` link skips a `null`: a plain
  link after one reads what it is given, so `a?.next.value` with a nullable
  `next` is `` Cannot read property `value` of `Node | null`; a link of a `?.` chain that may be `null` needs a `?.` of its own: `a?.next?.value` ``
  (`reject_optional_chain_link_nullable`). `?.` on a receiver that cannot
  be `null`, `this`, a narrowed local or a builtin namespace, is
  `` `a` is never `null` here, so `?.` has nothing to skip: write `.` ``
  (`reject_optional_chain_never_null`, `reject_optional_chain_narrowed`,
  `reject_optional_chain_this`, `reject_optional_chain_namespace`). `?.[i]`
  and `f?.()` stay refused (`reject_optional_chain_element`,
  `reject_optional_call`), a chain that ends in an element read is the
  element-read refusal above (`reject_optional_chain_element_last`), and one
  that ends in `get` is
  `` `h?.counts.get("a")` ends a `?.` chain in `get`: give the map a default first, then default what `get` answers ``
  (`reject_optional_chain_map_get`). Each `?.` lowers to an `icmp eq` against
  `null` and a branch to `nullish.default`, which every link shares, and runs
  nothing after a `null` link, an argument included. What a chain proves about
  an index holds only where its links ran, so a read after the `??` keeps its
  check (`optional_chain_bounds`). A call in a chain is held to every rule a
  call is (`reject_optional_chain_lock`, `reject_optional_chain_channel`), and
  a `Secret` either operand of the `??` makes is refused as one nobody owns
  (`reject_optional_chain_secret`).
- **Attributes**: a nullable parameter or return loses `nonnull` and
  `dereferenceable`; `align 8`, `readonly` and `nocapture` follow the usual
  rules ([ARCHITECTURE.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md#attribute-soundness-rules)).

## Discriminated unions

A union of two or more **variants**, `type Shape = Circle | Square | Tri`, is a
pointer to whichever variant it holds, and its first field says which. A
variant is a class or an interface whose first field is its **tag**: a field
of an [enum member type](declarations.md#enums), conventionally
`readonly kind: Kind.Circle = Kind.Circle` (`tests/cases/union_types`,
`tests/link/union_export` across modules).

```ts
enum Kind {
  Circle,
  Square,
}
class Circle {
  readonly kind: Kind.Circle = Kind.Circle;
  r: i32 = 1;
}
class Square {
  readonly kind: Kind.Square = Kind.Square;
  side: i32 = 2;
}
type Shape = Circle | Square;
const label = (s: Shape): string => (s.kind === Kind.Circle ? "circle" : "square");
```

Typed JSON reads and writes a union of classes by its tag ([Typed JSON](builtins.md#typed-json-nishjson-typed)).

**Layout.** Every union is the one LLVM type `%union.tagged = type { i32 }`,
behind a pointer. Every variant begins with its `i32` tag, so a variant
pointer is a union pointer by a `bitcast`, and reading the tag is a
`getelementptr` to field 0 and a load, whichever variant is there:

```llvm
%4 = bitcast %struct.Circle* %3 to %union.tagged*
...
%0 = getelementptr inbounds %union.tagged, %union.tagged* %s, i32 0, i32 0
%1 = load i32, i32* %0, align 4
```

`Shape | null` is the same pointer with `null` allowed, as
[Nullable types](#nullable-types) are.

**What makes a variant.** Each rule is checked where the union is spelled,
and each has its own code:

- A variant is a class or an interface that is not generic, so
  `type R = Ring<i32>` named in a union is
  `` `Ring<i32>` cannot be a union variant: a variant is a class or an interface that is not generic, because its tag is a field it declares itself ``
  (NL2522, `reject_union_generic_variant`). A generic type spelled with its
  arguments inside the union, `Circle | Ring<i32>`, and a member that is a
  scalar, an enum or an alias of one get the general refusal,
  `` Union types other than `T | null` are forbidden in Nish (values have one fixed layout) ``
  (NL1053, `reject_union_inline_generic`, `reject_union_untagged_scalar`,
  `reject_union_enum_alias_member`, `reject_union_scalar_alias_member`,
  `reject_union_type`).
- Its first field is of one enum member type: otherwise
  `` `Point` cannot be a union variant: its first field must be its tag, a field whose type is one member of an enum, such as `readonly kind: Kind.Circle = Kind.Circle` ``
  (NL2523, `reject_union_untagged`, `reject_paren_union_type`). A first
  field typed with its whole enum, `readonly kind: Kind = Kind.A`, holds a tag
  but types it as every variant's, so the union could not tell its variants
  apart by it; that is NL2559, which names the member to write:
  `` `First` cannot be a union variant: its tag `kind` has the whole enum `Kind` as its type, which every variant shares, so give it the one member it holds instead: `readonly kind: Kind.A = Kind.A` ``
  (`reject_union_tag_whole_enum`).
- The tag is `readonly`: otherwise
  `` `Circle` cannot be a union variant: its tag `kind` must be `readonly`, because the union tells its variants apart by it ``
  (NL2535, `reject_union_mutable_tag`).
- All the tags come from one enum (NL2524, `reject_union_mixed_enums`), the
  tag field has one name in every variant (NL2525, `reject_union_tag_names`),
  and no two variants share a tag (NL2526, `reject_union_duplicate_tag`).
- A union names at least two different variants, after aliases and nested
  unions are flattened: `Circle | Circle` is NL2527
  (`reject_union_one_variant`).

**Where a union goes.** A union is the type of a local, a parameter, a
field, a return, an array element (`Shape[]`, `Shape[][]`, or the members
spelled in place, `(Circle | Square)[]`), or of any of those made nullable,
and a `Map`'s value is any of those: `Map<string, Shape>`,
`Map<string, Shape[]>`, `Map<string, Shape | null>` (`union_map_value`).
A union is also a type argument: a generic class's (`Box<Shape>`,
`Box<Box<Shape>>`, `Stack<Shape>`, `union_generic_class`), a generic
function's or method's type parameter bound to one by its arguments
(`union_generic_call`), either side of a `Result`, `Result<Shape, E>` and
`Result<T, Shape>` (`union_result`), and `nish/map`'s `getOrInsert` and
`reserve` on a `Map<K, Shape>` (`union_map_helpers`). The instance is
monomorphised as for any other type argument, so `Box<Shape>` is laid out as
a class with a `Shape` field would be, and a `T` slot holds the union's one
pointer.
An alias may name another union, which is flattened: with `type Round =
Circle | Square`, `type Shape = Round | Tri` is the three variants. A value
of a variant, or of a union whose variants are all the wider union's,
converts to the union wherever the union is expected: an argument, a
`return`, an array literal under a `Shape[]` annotation, a `push`, a ternary
arm or a `??` default whose other side is the union
(`tests/cases/union_forms`), and the same places where a generic's `T` is
the union: a constructor's or a generic call's argument, `Ok(new Circle())`
in a function that returns `Result<Shape, E>` (`union_generic_class`,
`union_generic_call`, `union_result`). Equality on two unions compares the pointers, as
on any object.

**Reading.** The tag is the one member a union has until a test of the tag
narrows it (below): any other field or method is
`` `r` cannot be used on the union `Circle | Square`: a union has only its tag `kind` until a test of the tag narrows it to one variant ``
(NL2528, `reject_union_member_field`, `reject_union_method_call`, even when
every variant has it). It reads as the enum, `Kind`, so it compares, switches
and is passed as one. A union is read-only: a write through it is NL2529, even
to a field every variant has (`reject_union_assign_tag`).

**Comparisons that cannot be true.** As in `tsc`, comparing the tag with a
member no variant has is an error: `s.kind === Kind.Tri` when no variant is
tagged `Kind.Tri` is NL2531 (`reject_union_disjoint_compare`), and
`case Kind.Tri:` in a `switch (s.kind)` is NL2532
(`reject_union_disjoint_case`).

**Narrowing.** A test of a variable's tag narrows the variable, as in `tsc`.
Where `s.kind === Kind.Circle` holds, `s` reads as a `Circle`, so its fields
and methods are there; where it fails, `s` is the union of the variants left,
and when one variant is left it reads as that one
(`tests/cases/union_narrowing`):

```ts
const area = (s: Shape): i32 => {
  if (s.kind === Kind.Circle) {
    return 3 * s.r * s.r;
  }
  return s.side * s.side;
};
```

- The test narrows the branch it guards: the `then` and `else` of an `if`,
  the arms of a ternary, the right side of `&&` (where it held) and of `||`
  (where it failed), and the statements after an `if` whose branch always
  leaves (`return`, `break`, `continue`, a `panic(...)`). `!==` narrows the other way
  round, and the operands may be either way round, `Kind.Square === s.kind`.
- Each `case Kind.X:` of a `switch (s.kind)` narrows `s` to its variant, and
  `default` to the variants no `case` named. A `case` that a previous one falls
  through into narrows nothing.
- A null test composes with it: on `s: Shape | null`,
  `s !== null && s.kind === Kind.Circle && s.r > 0` reads `s.r`.
- Where an `||` held, either side may have made it hold, so the variable is
  what either side proved: past `s.kind === Kind.Circle || s.kind ===
  Kind.Square`, `s` is a `Circle | Square`, which has only its tag and whose
  tag is not `Kind.Tri`. The same goes for the side of an `&&` where it
  failed, for an enum variable, for any number of arms and for `===` mixed
  with `!==`; an arm that tests something else leaves the variable as
  declared (`tests/cases/union_narrowing_join`; `reject_union_narrow_or_if`,
  `reject_union_narrow_or_ternary`, `reject_union_narrow_and_false`,
  `reject_enum_narrow_or_if`, `reject_enum_narrow_or_ternary`,
  `reject_enum_narrow_or_three`, `reject_enum_narrow_or_mixed`,
  `reject_enum_narrow_and_false`).
- The test may read the variable through an assignment, which answers the
  value it stored: `(t = next()).kind === Kind.Square` narrows `t`, as
  `(k = next()) === Kind.A` narrows an enum `k`
  (`reject_union_narrow_test_assign`, `reject_union_narrow_or_assign`,
  `reject_enum_narrow_assign`).
- The variable is a parameter or a `let` or `const` local; a narrowed `const`
  stays narrowed in a data-parallel arrow that reads it
  (`tests/link/union_narrowing_capture`). An
  assignment to it drops what the tests proved, as for a nullable
  and a loop that assigns it drops it before its body
  (`reject_union_narrow_dropped`, `reject_union_narrow_else_assign`,
  `reject_union_narrow_loop_assign`).
- What a test proved holds past the statement that made it as far as every
  way out of it agrees, as in `tsc`. After an `if` with an `else`, the
  variable is what the arms that fall through left it, joined; after an
  `if` whose one arm falls through, what that arm left, so a chain of `else
  if`s whose branches all return leaves the variant no test named and an arm
  that assigns the variable leaves what it assigned
  (`reject_union_narrow_else_if_chain`, `reject_union_narrow_arm_assign`,
  `reject_nullable_arm_assign`). A block's early return narrows what follows
  the block. An enum local that an `if`, a ternary, a loop or a `switch`
  stores a member into holds, after it, what it held before or any member
  stored (`reject_enum_held_if_join`, `reject_enum_held_else_join`,
  `reject_enum_held_ternary`, `reject_enum_held_ternary_assign`,
  `reject_enum_held_loop_join`, `reject_enum_held_switch_join`). The join
  after an `if` covers every local and path either arm assigns, one first
  assigned in the `else` included (`reject_union_narrow_path_if_join`,
  `reject_union_narrow_path_if_test`), and every one a test inside either arm
  narrowed, whether or not an arm assigns it: two arms that each leave when
  `k === Kind.A` leave `k` not `Kind.A` past the `if`, joined with what held
  before it (`tests/cases/union_narrowing_tested_join`;
  `reject_enum_if_tested_join`, `reject_union_narrow_if_tested_join`,
  `reject_union_narrow_path_tested_join`, `reject_union_narrow_nullable_tested_join`,
  `reject_enum_else_if_tested_join`, `reject_enum_if_tested_outer`). A `switch` joins what each of its
  exits leaves: every `break` out of it, the fall off its last clause and,
  when no `default` covers every member, the case no clause matches; a
  clause that returns is no exit (`tests/cases/union_narrowing_switch_join`;
  `reject_union_narrow_path_switch`, `reject_union_narrow_path_switch_late`,
  `reject_enum_switch_join`, `reject_enum_switch_unmatched`), a variable only
  its clauses' tests narrowed included (`reject_enum_switch_tested_join`,
  `reject_enum_switch_tag_tested_join`). What held
  before the `switch` holds again at the start of each clause and in the
  case no label matches, whatever an earlier clause stored
  (`reject_union_narrow_switch_kept`, `reject_enum_switch_kept`). A loop is
  followed to a fixpoint, as `tsc` follows it: the head of a `while`, `for`
  or `do` holds what reaches it before the loop, at the end of an iteration
  and at a `continue` (through its update, for a `for`), joined until it no
  longer changes; after a `while` or `for` comes the head with its condition
  false, joined with every `break`,
  after a `do` the end of the body and its `continue`s with the condition
  false, and after a `for...of` the head and the `break`s. A loop inside the
  body and a `switch` inside it are followed the same way, an `if` or a
  `switch` narrowing its arms and clauses inside the loop as it does outside
  one (`tests/cases/union_narrowing_loop_flow`,
  `tests/cases/union_narrowing_loop_reads`; `reject_union_loop_while_join`,
  `reject_union_loop_do_join`, `reject_union_loop_condition_reassigned`,
  `reject_enum_loop_for_join`, `reject_enum_loop_do_join`,
  `reject_enum_loop_top_of_body`, `reject_enum_loop_do_continue`,
  `reject_enum_loop_break`, `reject_enum_loop_for_of`,
  `reject_enum_loop_nested`, `reject_enum_loop_switch`,
  `reject_enum_loop_switch_store`, `reject_enum_loop_switch_while`,
  `reject_union_loop_switch`). A variable the loop only tests, never
  writes, is followed too (`reject_enum_loop_tested_while`,
  `reject_enum_loop_tested_do`, `reject_enum_loop_tested_break`,
  `reject_enum_loop_tested_inner`, `reject_enum_loop_switch_tested`,
  `reject_union_loop_tested_while`, `reject_union_loop_null_tested`). A
  store holds what its value holds where the value is one of: a member; a
  local of a member type, `const m: Kind.B`; a call of a function that
  returns a member type; a field of a member type, or a call of a method
  that returns one, read through `this`, a local or parameter or a field of
  one, nullable or not; a `const` the loop declares once, read by its
  initializer; another
  enum variable; a union's tag; or a ternary of two of these, each arm read
  on its side of the condition
  (`reject_enum_loop_ternary_store`, `reject_enum_loop_copy_store`,
  `reject_union_loop_tag_copy`, `reject_enum_loop_member_local`,
  `reject_enum_loop_member_call`, `reject_enum_loop_field_store`,
  `reject_enum_loop_method_store`, `reject_enum_loop_nullable_receiver`,
  `reject_enum_loop_body_const`,
  `reject_enum_loop_ternary_narrowed`, `reject_enum_loop_ternary_tracked`,
  `reject_enum_loop_ternary_self`). A test against a member, a local of a
  member type or such a call narrows as outside a loop, and so does a test
  against another enum variable, by the members it holds there
  (`reject_enum_loop_const_test`, `reject_union_loop_const_test`,
  `reject_enum_loop_held_operand`, `reject_enum_loop_held_single`,
  `reject_enum_loop_held_ternary`, `reject_union_loop_held_operand`;
  `tests/cases/enum_loop_held_several`). A `for`
  update runs after the body and before the next test, and is followed
  there (`tests/cases/enum_loop_for_update`;
  `reject_enum_loop_for_update_store`, `reject_enum_loop_for_update_cond`),
  and is checked when the body is one refused statement, so both errors are
  reported (`reject_for_update_after_body`). A store of any other value holds
  the whole declared type. Where the loop holds a shape the fixpoint does not
  follow, a local or path holds, after it and throughout it, every member
  stored anywhere in it, which may be more than `tsc` knows ("Accepted here,
  refused by `tsc`", below).
- A tag compared with an enum variable narrows on the side where they are
  equal: `s.kind === k`, with `k` holding `Kind.Circle | Kind.Square`, makes
  `s` a `Circle | Square` there, and `j === k` leaves the enum `j` one of
  `k`'s members. Where they differ, nothing is known, since `k` may hold
  either, unless `k` holds one member, which is then left out
  (`tests/cases/union_narrowing_arms`;
  `reject_union_narrow_tag_variable`, `reject_enum_compare_variable`).
- A tag tested through a path — a field `h.k`, `this.k`, a field of a field
  `h.s.kind`, a literal index `xs[0].kind` — stays narrowed for the
  comparisons after it, so a repeat test of a member already excluded is
  NL2531, as `tsc`'s TS2367 is. A store to the path, to a prefix of it
  (`h.s = t`, `xs[0] = t`) or to its root drops what it held, and the joins
  above follow a path as they follow a variable; a call does not, as in
  `tsc` (`tests/cases/union_narrowing_paths`;
  `reject_union_narrow_path_field`, `reject_union_narrow_path_this`,
  `reject_union_narrow_path_nested`, `reject_union_narrow_path_index`,
  `reject_union_narrow_path_join`, `reject_union_narrow_path_loop`). An
  index is part of the path when it names one element, as TypeScript 5.5
  reads it: a number literal, a parameter, a `const` (`const i = 0` makes
  `xs[i]` the path `xs[0]`, annotated or not, and so does `const j = i`
  after an unannotated `const i = 0`, whose type is the literal `0`), a module
  constant (`const IDX: i32 = 0` makes `xs[IDX]` the path `xs[0]` too, and
  `const A: i32 = -1` and `const B: i32 = -1` make `xs[A]` and `xs[B]` one
  path), or a `let` nothing in its block assigns, a closure's body included. A
  `let` that is assigned or stepped (`i = 1`, `i++`), a parenthesised name or any
  other expression keys no path, so `xs[i]` is not narrowed through it, and a
  store through such an index (`xs[j] = t`) drops nothing, as in `tsc`
  (`tests/cases/union_narrowing_index`, `union_narrowing_index_const`;
  `reject_union_narrow_path_ident`, `reject_union_narrow_path_steady`,
  `reject_union_narrow_path_const_index`,
  `reject_union_narrow_path_index_store`,
  `reject_union_narrow_path_const_chain`,
  `reject_union_narrow_path_negative_index`,
  `reject_union_narrow_path_negative_zero`,
  `reject_union_narrow_path_module_index`,
  `reject_union_narrow_path_module_literal`,
  `reject_union_narrow_path_module_ident`,
  `reject_union_narrow_path_module_negative`). The union read through the path is
  not narrowed (below).
- A union of two or more variants left still has only its tag
  (`reject_union_narrow_none_if`, `reject_union_narrow_none_ternary`,
  `reject_union_narrow_none_and`, `reject_union_narrow_none_or`,
  `reject_union_narrow_none_fallthrough`), and a narrowed variant has only its
  own fields (`reject_union_narrow_none_case`, `reject_union_narrow_none_null`,
  `reject_union_narrow_none_reversed`).

What a test excluded stays excluded, so a second test of a tag already ruled
out is always false and NL2531, in an `if`, a ternary or an `&&`
(`reject_union_narrow_second_if`, `reject_union_narrow_second_ternary`,
`reject_union_narrow_second_and`), and so is its `case`, NL2532
(`reject_union_narrow_dead_case`). An enum local holds what it was given: the
tag stored in a local, `const k: Kind = s.kind`, holds only the variants'
members, and a local given `Kind.Circle` holds only that member until it is
assigned again, so `k === Kind.Tri` against a member it cannot hold is NL2531
and `case Kind.Tri:` of a `switch (k)` NL2532, as `tsc`'s TS2367 and TS2678 are
(`reject_union_tag_local_compare`, `reject_union_tag_local_case`,
`reject_enum_held_const`, `reject_enum_held_let`, `reject_enum_held_reassign`,
`reject_union_tag_held_capture`).

A test of an enum variable against a member narrows what it holds in the same
forms, as `tsc` narrows it: `k === Kind.A` and `k !== Kind.A`, either way
round, in an `if` and its `else`, a ternary, `&&` and `||`, after an `if` whose
branch always leaves, and each `case` and the `default` of a `switch (k)`. This
holds for a parameter `k: Kind` as for the tag local `const k: Kind = s.kind`,
and an assignment drops it as it drops a union's. So after
`if (k === Kind.A) return`, `k === Kind.A` is NL2531 and `case Kind.A:` NL2532,
as `tsc`'s TS2367 and TS2678 are (`tests/cases/enum_narrowing`;
`reject_enum_narrow_else`, `reject_enum_narrow_early`,
`reject_enum_narrow_ternary`, `reject_enum_narrow_and`,
`reject_enum_narrow_or`, `reject_enum_narrow_switch`,
`reject_enum_narrow_tag_local`). Narrowed to one member, the variable is that
member's type, so `let j = k` is a `Kind.A` that `j = Kind.B` does not fit
(`reject_enum_narrow_let_member`), as in `tsc`.

A `switch` whose subject reads a union variant's tag field, with no
`default` and labels that name every variant the tag can hold, is
**complete**: no value reaches the case no label
names, so when no `break` targets the `switch` and its last clause leaves, the
`switch` terminates (see Termination) and can end a function that returns a
value, as in `tsc`. Its unmatched case compiles to LLVM's `unreachable`. The
tag may be read through a union variable, a field, an element or a call's
result, `s.kind`, `h.shape.kind`, `shapes[i].kind`, and a variable that a test
before the `switch` left fewer variants needs labels for those only
(`tests/cases/union_switch`). With a variant unnamed, the `switch` does not
terminate, and a function that returns a value and ends in it is the
missing-return error, as `tsc --strict --noImplicitReturns`'s TS2366 is
(`reject_union_switch_missing_case`, `reject_union_switch_missing_case_field`).
Complete means the tag can hold nothing else: a variant's tag is `readonly`,
written only with its own member, and a union never crosses the interop
boundary, so no other `i32` reaches it.

**Stricter than TypeScript.** Each of these programs is accepted by
`tsc --strict` and refused here; each refusal is pinned:

- **No narrowing by assignment.** `tsc` narrows a union-typed slot to the
  type of the value last stored in it, so after `let s: Shape = new Circle()`
  it treats `s` as a `Circle`. This version does not track that, so a store
  of a value that is only some of the variants into a union local, field,
  element or nullable union is NL2534, and asks for the variant's own type or
  a value of the whole union (`reject_union_narrow_const`,
  `reject_union_narrow_assign`, `reject_union_narrow_field`,
  `reject_union_narrow_element`, `reject_union_narrow_ternary`,
  `reject_union_narrow_nullable`). A call that returns `Shape` is a value of
  the whole union, and is stored freely. Passing and returning a variant
  narrows nothing, and is accepted. A test of the tag does narrow (above).
- **A union is a type argument, but not a key.** `Box<Shape>`, a generic
  function or method whose type parameter binds to a union, `Result<Shape, E>`
  / `Result<T, Shape>` and `nish/map`'s helpers on a `Map<K, Shape>` are
  accepted (above), as in `tsc`. Three things stay refused, each under its own
  rule: a union is not a `Map` or `Set` key, which is the key rule's refusal
  (NL2353, `reject_union_map_key`, `reject_union_set`); a generic class is
  not a variant (NL2522, `reject_union_generic_variant`); and a store of a
  bare variant into a generic instance's union field, `b.value = new
  Square()` on a `Box<Shape>`, is NL2534 as into any union field
  (`reject_union_generic_field_store`). A union does not meet a constraint
  (`<T extends HasKind>`, NL2328, `reject_union_generic_constraint`), and an instance
  over a union is not key material for `nish:secret`
  (NL2428, `reject_union_generic_secret`), nor a class typed JSON writes
  (NL2486, `reject_union_generic_json`), nor something a C header or N-API bridge
  spells (`reject_union_generic_export`, `reject_union_result_export`).
- **No inferred unions.** A union is never inferred: an unannotated ternary
  or array literal of two variants is the existing same-type refusal
  (`reject_union_ternary_inferred`, `reject_union_array_inferred`; so is
  one a generic call would bind `T` to, `first([new Square(), new Circle()])`,
  `reject_union_generic_inferred`), an arrow
  returning one needs its annotation (`reject_union_arrow_result`), and a
  local initialised from the tag without an annotation, `const k = s.kind`
  or the tag in a `for…of`, is NL2530, because `tsc` would infer the union
  of the tags' member types, which this version does not have
  (`reject_union_inferred_tag`, `reject_union_forof_tag`). So is the tag as
  an element of an unannotated array literal, an arm of an unannotated
  ternary, or the result of an arrow that binds a type parameter
  (`reject_union_tag_array`, `reject_union_tag_ternary`,
  `reject_union_tag_arrow`). An annotation as the enum, `const k: Kind =
  s.kind`, is accepted, and the local holds the variants' members (above).
  An enum variable narrowed to two or more members is the same: `const j = k`
  after `if (k === Kind.A) return` is NL2530, since `tsc` would infer
  `Kind.B | Kind.C` (`reject_enum_narrow_inferred_set`); annotate it as `Kind`.
- **No narrowing of a union through a path.** `tsc` narrows a property
  path, `h.s.kind === Kind.Circle` then `h.s.r`; this version narrows the
  tag read through the path (above) but the union only in a variable, so a
  read of a variant's member through the path is
  `` `r` cannot be used on the union `Circle | Square | Tri` read through a property path: a test of the tag narrows a variable, not a path, so copy the union into a local first and test that ``
  (NL2558, `reject_union_narrow_path`).
- **A complete `switch` reads the union's tag.** `tsc` treats a `switch`
  whose labels name every member of an enum as complete, and so ends a
  function in it; this version does so for a union's tag only (above). A
  plain enum, `switch (k)` for `k: Kind`, can arrive from C holding any
  `i32`, so a `switch` on a plain `Kind` local or field is never complete
  (`reject_union_switch_enum`), nor is one on the tag copied into an enum
  local, `const k: Kind = s.kind`, or a `let` one reassigned on another path
  (`reject_union_switch_tag_local`, `reject_union_switch_tag_local_reassigned`).
  A narrowed path needs every tag of the whole union: `switch (h.s.kind)`
  after `if (h.s.kind === Kind.A) return` is complete only with `Kind.A`
  labelled too, since a call between the test and the `switch` could have
  reassigned `h.s` (`reject_union_switch_path_narrowed`); a narrowed union
  local, which nothing reassigns unseen, is complete with the labels of the
  variants left to it (`tests/cases/union_switch_narrowed`). Nor is a `switch`
  complete on an enum field assigned from
  a tag, `b.k = s.kind`, which a call, an alias, a method or `this` can
  overwrite with any member (`reject_union_switch_enum_field_call` and its
  siblings): what decides is the subject's static type, a union's tag field,
  never what a path was assigned or narrowed to hold. End such a function
  after the `switch`, or give it a `default` (`tests/cases/union_switch_flow`).
- **No `never`.** Where the tests have excluded every variant, `tsc` types the
  variable `never` and accepts a read of it; this version has no such type, so
  the read is
  `` `s` has no variant left here: the tests before this read excluded every variant of its union, which TypeScript types `never` and this version has no type for ``
  (NL2557, `reject_union_narrow_exhausted`).
- **No narrowing through a stored condition.** `tsc` narrows `s` where a
  `const` holding a test of its tag is true, `const round = s.kind ===
  Kind.Circle; if (round) { s.r }`; this version narrows on the test
  itself only, so `s.r` there reads the union (NL2528,
  `reject_union_narrow_aliased`). Test the tag in the condition.
- **No field shared by every variant.** `tsc` reads a field every variant
  declares through the union; this version reads only the tag before a test
  narrows it (NL2528, `reject_union_member_field`).
- **A tag of one member.** `tsc` accepts a variant whose tag is typed with its
  whole enum, `readonly kind: Kind = Kind.A`, which then discriminates
  nothing; this version asks for the member type (NL2559,
  `reject_union_tag_whole_enum`).
- **No covariant arrays.** A `Circle[]` is not a `Shape[]`, since a push
  through the wider type would put a `Square` among the circles; build the
  array as a `Shape[]` (`reject_union_covariant_array`).
- **No object literal of a union.** An object literal where a union is
  wanted, `area({ kind: Kind.Tri, base: 2 })` for a `Circle | Tri`
  parameter, has no one class to build (`reject_union_object_literal`):
  build it into a local annotated as the interface, `const t: Tri = { ... }`,
  and pass that.
- **No `new Array<Shape>(n)`**, which would fill the array with a zero no
  variant is (`reject_union_new_array`).
- **No class for its interface variant.** A class that implements an
  interface variant is not itself a variant, so `tsc` accepts a `Band
  implements Ring` where `Circle | Ring` is wanted and this version does not
  (`reject_union_implements_variant`): convert it to the interface first,
  `const r: Ring = new Band()`.
- **A readonly tag.** `tsc` accepts a variant whose tag can be reassigned;
  this version asks for `readonly` (NL2535, `reject_union_mutable_tag`).
- **No write through the union.** `tsc` accepts `s.x = 1` when every variant
  has `x`; this version refuses every write through a union (NL2529,
  `reject_union_assign_tag`).

A union is not a class either, so `new Shape()` names no constructor, as in
`tsc` (`reject_union_new`). A value of any other type where a union is
wanted is the existing refusal of its position (`reject_union_into_init`,
`reject_union_into_assign`, `reject_union_into_arg`,
`reject_union_into_push`, `reject_union_into_index`,
`reject_union_into_nullable`, `reject_union_field_other`,
`reject_union_return_other`, `reject_union_method_arg`,
`reject_union_ctor_arg`, `reject_union_array_other`,
`reject_union_ternary_other`, `reject_union_nullish_other`). A smaller union
stored where a larger one is declared narrows it in `tsc`, as a variant
does, and is NL2534 too (`reject_union_narrow_subunion`).

**Accepted here, refused by `tsc`.** The loop pass (above) reads less than
`tsc` in the shapes below, and these are all of them: a variable holds every
member stored anywhere in the loop, or its whole declared type, so a
comparison `tsc` refuses as TS2367 may compile here. Each is pinned as it
stands, with the expected `tsc` error written at the comparison, so the case
fails on either side once the gap closes (`tests/cases/enum_loop_join_gap`):

- **A path.** A tag or enum held by a field, `h.k`, is joined over the whole
  loop, not followed through it.
- **A store inside an expression.** An assignment that is an argument,
  `keep((j = Kind.C))`, an initializer, `const t = (j = Kind.C)`, or the
  inner store of a chain, `k = j = Kind.C`, rather than a statement of its
  own.
- **A value the pass cannot read.** A store of a field or a method call
  read through anything but `this`, a local or parameter the loop does not
  declare, or a field of one — an element, `j = gs[0].b` or
  `j = gs[0].pick()`, a call's result, `j = makeG().b`, a receiver the loop
  declares, `const g = new G(); j = g.b` — holds the whole declared type,
  though the field or method is typed with one member. So does a store of a
  `let` the loop declares, or of a `const` it declares from a tracked
  variable, as the swap `const t: Kind = a; a = b; b = t;` does.
- **An arm that holds nothing.** A ternary arm that reads the stored
  variable where the condition leaves it no member, the `k` of
  `k = k === Kind.A ? Kind.B : k` while `k` holds only `Kind.A`, reads as
  the whole type, as the checker reads a variable narrowed to `never`, so
  the store holds every member from then on.
- **A wide type.** A union of more than 29 variants or an enum of more than
  29 members.

`try` is refused by Nish on its own, a destructuring pattern only ever
declares fresh names rather than storing to a variable (a destructuring
assignment is NL2773, [Destructuring declarations](statements.md#destructuring-declarations)),
and an arrow may read a local it captures but never
assign it (NL2586, [Function parameters](declarations.md#function-parameters)), so no loop
that compiles stores through any of them. A loop that holds a
labelled statement or a labelled `break` or `continue` anywhere in its body,
or whose `switch` has a clause that falls into the next, is one the pass
gives up on: it keeps the checker's widened state.

**Across a sidecar.** A union has no C spelling yet, so a function exported
through `--emit-header` or `--emit-napi` whose parameter or return holds a
union is refused, and so is a union-holding field of any class or interface
the compilation declares, exported or not, under a flag that lays the classes
out as C structs (`--emit-header`, `--emit-napi`, `--emit-napi-async`): a
header lays out every class and interface of the program, a private one too
(`reject_union_private_field`). A build with `--emit-dts` alone describes no
class, so there a union field of a class only the module reads — root
storage's graph among them — is accepted; a union in an exported function's
parameter or result is still refused under every sidecar flag. The message is
`` `tagOf`'s parameter `s` is `Circle | Square`, which holds a union no sidecar can describe: a union has no C spelling in this version ``
(NL4009, `reject_union_export_param`, `reject_union_export_return`,
`reject_union_export_field`, `reject_union_export_array_field`). Unions
cross Nish modules freely (`tests/link/union_export`).
